The wind did not merely blow; it screamed. It was a high-pitched, tearing shriek that seemed to strip the very soul from the air, carrying with it a slurry of ice and salt that stung the skin like broken glass. The lighthouse stood as a solitary sentinel against the churning chaos of the North Atlantic, its white-painted stone facade battered by the relentless assault of the winter gale. It was not a static object but a living thing, groaning under the weight of the elements, its foundation vibrating with a deep, resonant hum that traveled up through the concrete and into the bones of anyone who dared to stand within its walls.

Below, the sea was a monstrous entity, no longer water but a wall of black, frothing fury. Waves the size of houses rose from the depths, their crests turning into mist before they crashed against the jagged rocks with the force of artillery fire. The spray reached the gallery, a hundred feet above the waterline, turning the air into a freezing fog that obscured the horizon. The world had shrunk to the immediate vicinity of the tower, a small, illuminated bubble of safety in an ocean of darkness and violence.
